original_question: Determine whether there exists a convex body S in R^3 for which the following Kakeya rotation property fails: whenever K is a convex body containing a rotated translate of S in every orientation, not every two copies of S inside K can be continuously rotated into one another while remaining inside K.
target_in_paper: arXiv:2310.18163, Section 9, Question 9.2, which isolates the open 3-dimensional case of the Kakeya rotation problem; this is the same problem stated more fully as Question 5.1 in the cited paper Rotation inside convex Kakeya sets.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the ambient dimension R^3, the object sought (a convex body S), the S-Kakeya hypothesis on a containing convex body K (copies of S in every orientation), and the conclusion of interest: failure of the ability to continuously rotate one copy of S into another while staying inside K. It is therefore clearly aimed at the 3-dimensional counterexample question singled out after the paper's summary theorem.
missing_details: The main logical correction is a quantifier issue: the paper asks whether there exists some convex body S in R^3 for which there exists some convex S-Kakeya body K in R^3 containing two S-copies that cannot be rotated into one another within K. Your wording can be read as saying that for every such K the failure occurs, which is stronger than the paper's question.
A convex body should be made explicit as a non-empty compact convex subset of R^3; the paper also notes that a body means a non-empty compact set.
The ambient field is the reals, and the relevant orientations are rotations rho in SO(3).
The S-Kakeya condition should be formalized: for every rotation rho in SO(3), there exists a translation vector w in R^3 such that rho(S)+w is contained in K.
The two copies under comparison should be specified as rho_0(S)+w_0 and rho_1(S)+w_1 inside the same convex body K.

The phrase 'can be continuously rotated into one another within K' should be formalized by continuous maps gamma:[0,1]->SO(3) and delta:[0,1]->R^3 with gamma(i)=rho_i and delta(i)=w_i for i=0,1, and gamma(t)(S)+delta(t) contained in K for all t in [0,1].
The paper packages this condition with the defined shorthand 'S has the Kakeya rotation property'; Question 9.2 asks for a convex body S in R^3 that does not have this property.

To stay faithful to the paper's scope, it is helpful to note the surrounding boundary cases established before the question: there is no 2-dimensional counterexample, unit line segments do have the property, and counterexamples exist in every dimension d>=4; the unresolved case is exactly d=3.
refined_question: Does there exist a non-empty compact convex set S subset of R^3 and a non-empty compact convex set K subset of R^3 such that K is S-Kakeya—that is, for every rotation rho in SO(3) there exists w in R^3 with rho(S)+w subset of K—but there are two S-copies rho_0(S)+w_0 and rho_1(S)+w_1 contained in K for which no continuous maps gamma:[0,1]->SO(3) and delta:[0,1]->R^3 satisfy gamma(0)=rho_0, gamma(1)=rho_1, delta(0)=w_0, delta(1)=w_1, and gamma(t)(S)+delta(t) subset of K for every t in [0,1]?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: does there exist a convex body S subset of R^3 that does not have the Kakeya rotation property?
justification: The nearest official formulation in arXiv:2310.18163 is Section 9, Question 9.2. Section 9 first defines what it means for K to be S-Kakeya and for two S-copies to be rotated into each other within K, then introduces the shorthand that S has the Kakeya rotation property when this always happens for convex S-Kakeya bodies K. Theorem 9.1 summarizes the known cases: the property holds in dimension 2 and for unit line segments, but counterexamples exist for every d>=4. The very next question asks whether there is a counterexample in R^3. Your draft is therefore targeting exactly that open problem, but it needs the quantifiers and the motion definition sharpened to match the paper.
